Let’s simplify step by step:

1. We see s0, s1, s2, s3 are all given true.  
2. The rule for wide is “wide is true if s0, s1, s2, s3 are all true,” so wide is definitely true.  
3. The rule for q is “q is true if v4 is true and wide is true.” Since wide is true, q is exactly equivalent to v4 being true.  
4. Now v4 and w4 are tied only by the rules  
     • v4 is true if w4 is not true, and  
     • w4 is true if v4 is not true.  
   That means v4 and w4 are simply perfect negations of each other, but there is no additional constraint fixing which one is true.  
5. No other non-“bad” rule pins down v4/w4, so v4 could consistently be either true or false.  

Therefore q could equally be true (if v4 is true) or false (if v4 is false). It cannot be decided from the given information.

We first observe that s0,s1,s2,s3 are all given true, so the rule

  wide :- s0,s1,s2,s3

yields wide = true.  Then

  q :- v4, wide

reduces to

  q :- v4

since wide is true.  Hence q is true exactly when v4 is true.

Now look only at the definitions of v4 and w4:

  v4 :- not w4.
  w4 :- not v4.

No other rules mention v4 or w4.  To prove v4 we must show not w4; but to show w4 we must show not v4, which in turn requires not w4 again, and so on in an infinite loop of negation‐as‐failure.  Neither not w4 nor not v4 can finitely succeed or finitely fail, so the query v4 (and hence q) does not terminate with a definite success or failure. Let’s restate the key points.  We have facts  
 s0, s1, s2, s3.  
Therefore wide ← s0, s1, s2, s3 makes wide true in every answer set.  
And  
 q ← v4, wide  
so q is exactly equivalent to v4 in any answer set.

All of v0…v7 and w0…w7 are defined by mutual defaults  
 vi ← not wi.  
 wi ← not vi.  
so in any answer set exactly one of {vi,wi} holds.  

The atom bad is defined by a host of rules  
 … ← (three positive literals) , not bad.  
If bad were ever included in a candidate, not bad would be false, no rule could derive bad, and the candidate would fail minimality.  Hence in every stable model bad must be false, and so we must avoid satisfying any of those “three‐literal” bodies simultaneously.  Equivalently, for each triple (ℓ1,ℓ2,ℓ3) in the bodies we must ensure ¬(ℓ1∧ℓ2∧ℓ3).

We only need one answer set with v4 = true to show “Definitely yes.”  A direct assignment that works is:

 v4 = true  
 v0 = true  
 v2 = true  
 v1 = v3 = v5 = v6 = v7 = false

Then wi = not vi for i=0…7, and one checks that no forbidden triple all become true.  In particular every bad‐rule body has at least one atom false, so bad remains false, and the usual minimality check for the reduct goes through.  In the resulting model wide is true (by the s‐facts) and v4 is true, so q is true.  

Therefore there is at least one answer set in which q holds.  

ANSWER: A

Let V = {v0…v7}, W = {w0…w7}.  Apart from the s‐ and wide/rules, each pair vi∕wi is defined by

 vi ← not wi.  
 wi ← not vi.

so in any stable model exactly one of vi, wi holds for each i=0…7.  The rule

 q ← v4, wide

(and facts s0…s3) makes wide true in every model, so q ⇔ v4.

All the “bad” rules have the form

 bad ← L1, L2, L3(, L4), not bad,

and are active only if all Li are true and bad is false.  A classical stable‐model check shows that (i) bad must be false in any stable model, and (ii) every “bad” rule’s body must be false.  These bodies are just forbidden combinations of some vi/wj.  

One can exhibit a full assignment choosing w4 (thus v4 false so q false) and making sure every bad‐body has at least one false literal.  For example:

 w4,w7,w1,w5,w3,w6 true;  
 v0,v2 true;  
 (all other vi/wj chosen to be the opposite).

One checks that no bad‐rule is then fired, so this is a stable model with v4 false (hence q false).  Likewise one easily gets a model with v4 true (hence q true).  Thus q holds in some but not all answer sets.

Let’s isolate the two relevant conditions for q:

1. wide is true if and only if s0 and s1 are both true. Since s0 and s1 are given true, wide is definitely true.  
2. v2 is defined by the pair of rules  
   • v2 is true if w2 is not true.  
   • w2 is true if v2 is not true.  

These two force v2 and w2 to be complementary, but do not pick out which one is actually true. Hence v2 may be true in one admissible interpretation and false in another. Because q requires v2 to be true but v2 is not forced, q itself is not forced.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s focus on q.  The only rule for q is  
  q ← v2, wide.  

We already know s0 and s1 are facts, so  
  wide ← s0, s1  
succeeds, hence wide is true.  Thus proving q reduces to proving v2.

Now look at v2 and w2:

  (1) v2 ← not w2.  
  (2) w2 ← not v2.  

To prove v2 we must show not w2.  That requires attempting to prove w2.  To prove w2 we must show not v2, which sends us back to proving v2.  This mutual negation‐as‐failure cycle never terminates, nor does it finitely fail.

Since the attempt to prove v2 (and thus q) neither succeeds nor finitely fails, under Prolog‐style negation‐as‐failure we cannot get a definite yes or no.

ANSWER: C

Let us first note that s0 and s1 are facts, so wide ← s0,s1 will always derive wide. Hence q ← v2,wide is in effect equivalent to q ← v2. So q holds exactly in those answer‐sets in which v2 is true.

Next observe the mutually recursive pair

  v2 ← not w2.  
  w2 ← not v2.

This is the standard even‐loop over negation which has exactly two stable models (answer‐sets) on {v2,w2}: one with v2 true, w2 false, and one with w2 true, v2 false. Hence, if the rest of the program does not rule out the “v2‐branch,” there will be an answer‐set in which v2 holds—and hence q holds.

All the many rules for bad have the form

  bad ← A,B,C,not bad.

In stable‐model semantics these become constraints: in any candidate where bad is initially false, if A,B,C all become true that candidate must include bad—but then none of those rules can fire, so the result fails minimality.  Thus valid answer‐sets must avoid making all three of A,B,C true in any such rule.  In other words the “bad”-rules impose a large—but by inspection not obviously unsatisfiable—set of constraints on the v’s and w’s, leaving one still free choice on each v_i∕w_i pair.  In particular one can choose the v2‐branch (v2=true, w2=false) and then carefully choose the other v_i and w_i so as to break every triple in the bad‐constraints.  Concretely, one can assign each of the other seven pairs so as to falsify at least one atom in each forbidden triple.  Thus there is indeed at least one full 8-pair assignment extending v2=true which satisfies all the bad-constraints.

Therefore the program admits at least one answer‐set in which v2 is true, hence q is true. Under credulous (brave) reasoning, q is true in at least one answer set.

ANSWER: A

Let’s first note the “choice‐pairs” of rules for w0/v0, w1/v1, …, w7/v7:

  w_i ← not v_i.  
  v_i ← not w_i.

In each case exactly one of {w_i, v_i} must appear in an answer set (the other is false).  Thus there are 2^8 = 256 ways to choose truth‐values for v0…v7 (and the corresponding w’s).

We also have

  s0, s1 are true.  
  wide ← s0, s1.  

so wide is always true.  Finally

  q ← v2, wide.

Since wide is always true, q holds exactly in those answer sets where v2 was chosen.  But half of the 256 answer sets choose w2 (making v2 false), so q fails there.

No constraints eliminate these “w2‐choices” (the many “bad”–rules only force bad = true when certain patterns occur; they do not forbid any v/w‐combination).  Hence there exist answer sets with q=false, and others with q=true.  Under skeptical (cautious) reasoning q is not in every answer set.  

ANSWER: B

Let’s isolate the relevant portion of the program:

1. s0.  
2. s1.  
3. wide ← s0, s1.  
4. v2 ← not w2.  
5. w2 ← not v2.  
6. q ← v2, wide.

Facts s0 and s1 are true, so by rule 3 wide is true.  
Rules 4–5 form a mutual negation cycle:

  – v2 is true exactly if w2 is false.  
  – w2 is true exactly if v2 is false.  

Under well‐founded semantics a simple negation‐cycle like this leaves both v2 and w2 undefined.  

Now consider q ← v2, wide.  We have wide = true but v2 = undefined, so the body v2∧wide evaluates to undefined.  Hence q has no rule whose body is founded‐true, nor is it defeated or grounded—it remains undefined.  

Conclusion: q is undefined under the well‐founded semantics.  

ANSWER: C

We observe first that in all herding of t‐rules:

  t₃ is true if v₁ is true  
  t₂ ← t₃  
  t₁ ← t₂  
  t₀ ← t₁  
  q  ← t₀  

so q ends up “on” exactly when v₁ is set to true.  But v₁ itself comes only from

  v₁ ← not w₁  
  w₁ ← not v₁  

so there are two perfectly symmetric assignments for (v₁,w₁): either v₁=1, w₁=0 or v₁=0, w₁=1.  No other rule forces v₁ one way or the other once we allow bad=true.  Indeed, if any “bad ← … ∧ not bad” rule fires then bad becomes true, which then blocks all further bad‐rules, leaving all the vᵢ,wᵢ otherwise free (modulo their own complement‐pairs).  

Thus one can build a model with v₁=1 (so q=1) and bad=true, and another model with v₁=0 (so q=0) and bad=true, both satisfying every implication.  Hence q is not fixed.  

ANSWER: C

We need to determine q.  q ← t0 ← t1 ← t2 ← t3 ← v1.  So q succeeds iff v1 succeeds.

v1 is defined by a single clause

 v1 ← not w1

and w1 by

 w1 ← not v1.

To prove v1 under Prolog’s negation‐as‐failure we must prove not w1, which calls w1, which must prove not v1, which calls v1 again.  This mutual negation leads to an infinite loop: there is no finite proof of v1 nor finite failure of v1.  Hence q neither succeeds nor finitely fails.  Under the operational closed‐world, neg‐as‐failure semantics, we cannot obtain a definite yes or no.

xᵢ = 1 means vᵢ true (wᵢ false), and xᵢ = 0 means vᵢ false (wᵢ true).  
Because of the mutual‐negation rules vᵢ←not wᵢ and wᵢ←not vᵢ, every answer set picks exactly one of vᵢ,wᵢ in each pair.  

The goal q holds iff t₀ holds iff t₁ holds iff t₂ holds iff t₃ holds iff v₁ holds, so q is credulously true iff there is an answer set with v₁ = true (x₁=1).  

All the “bad”‐rules are of the form  
  bad ← A, B, C, not bad  
and so in order to avoid inconsistency (“bad” cannot end up both false and forced true), one must choose the xᵢ so that **no** triple (A,B,C) is simultaneously true.  Each triple constraint becomes a clause forbidding that conjunction. A systematic case analysis on x₅ (0 or 1) shows that **no** satisfying assignment exists with x₁=1.  Hence in **every** answer set v₁ must be false, so q is false in **all** answer sets.

Let’s name the 8 choices (v0/w0,…,v7/w7) as independent even‐negation cycles:

  vX ← not wX  
  wX ← not vX  

For each X=0…7 we must choose either vX or wX.  No other rules force a particular choice for any of these eight.  

Next, t3←v1, t2←t3, t1←t2, t0←t1, q←t0.  
Thus q is true exactly when v1 is chosen; if w1 is chosen, then v1 is false and so q is false.

All the “bad”–rules simply say “bad ← (some triple of v’s or w’s) ∧ not bad.”  Any concrete assignment to the v’s and w’s will make at least one such triple body true, so bad will be derived in every answer set—but that does not interfere with the independent choice of v1 vs. w1.

Hence there are answer sets with v1 (and so q) true, and answer sets with w1 (and so q) false.  q is not true in every answer set.

ANSWER: B

Let’s trace the dependencies:

1. q is true iff t0 is true.  
2. t0 ← t1 ← t2 ← t3 ← v1.  
   So q’s truth reduces to the truth of v1.  
3. v1 is defined by the rule  
     v1 ← not w1,  
   while w1 is defined by  
     w1 ← not v1.  
   This is a classic even negation cycle. Under well‐founded semantics both v1 and w1 become undefined.  
4. Since v1 is undefined, t3, t2, t1, t0 and hence q are all undefined.  

Therefore q is neither definitely true nor definitely false.  

ANSWER: C

Let p4 stand for “v4,” w4 for “w4,” etc.  The chain for q is

1)  q is true iff t0 ∧ wide.  
2)  wide = s0 ∧ s1 = true ∧ true = true.  
3)  t0 ← t1 ← t2 ← t3 ← w4.  

Hence q = w4.  

But v4 and w4 are defined only by  
    w4 ↔ ¬v4  
    v4 ↔ ¬w4,  
so w4 (and v4) can consistently be either true or false without contradicting any of the other rules.  Therefore q can be either true or false.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s isolate q:

1. q :- t0, wide.
2. wide :- s0, s1.  
   And s0 and s1 are given true, so wide is definitely true.
3. t0 :- t1; t1 :- t2; t2 :- t3; t3 :- w4.  
   Hence t0 succeeds exactly if w4 succeeds.

So q succeeds exactly if w4 succeeds.

Now w4 is defined by a two‐way negation loop:

  w4 :- not v4.  
  v4 :- not w4.

Querying w4 triggers not v4, which calls v4, which in turn calls not w4, which calls w4 again, and so on. There is no terminating proof of w4 nor an unequivocal finite failure of w4—evaluation loops.

Therefore q’s truth cannot be determined by a terminating proof or finite failure under Prolog‐style negation‐as‐failure.

ANSWER: C

Let us reformulate the core of the problem.  We have these key definitions:

1.  q ⇐ t₀ ∧ wide.  
2.  wide ⇐ s₀ ∧ s₁.  
3.  s₀ and s₁ are facts (both true).  
4.  t₀ ⇐ t₁,  t₁ ⇐ t₂,  t₂ ⇐ t₃,  t₃ ⇐ w₄.  
5.  w₄ ⇐ ¬v₄  and  v₄ ⇐ ¬w₄.  (mutually exclusive choice: exactly one of v₄, w₄ must hold)  
6.  There are a large number of “bad”‐rules of the form  
      bad ⇐ B ∧ ¬bad  
   each B being a conjunction of three literals in {v₀…v₇,w₀…w₇}.  An answer set must make every such B false (so that bad remains false) by falsifying at least one literal in each B.  

Thus:

– wide is unconditionally true (since s₀ and s₁ are true).  
– In order to get t₀, we must pick w₄ true (so that t₃⇐w₄ fires, then t₂, t₁, t₀ all fire).  
– Once w₄ is true, q will follow as soon as t₀ is derived.  

All we need, for a “credulous” (brave) proof of q, is to exhibit at least one consistent choice of the mutually‐exclusive pairs  
   (v₀∨w₀), (v₁∨w₁), …, (v₇∨w₇), and (v₄∨w₄)  
that

  • Chooses w₄ (to get t₀ ⇒ q),  
  • And in which no “bad”–rule body B is left entirely true (so that bad cannot be forced).  

Although there are many such B’s, one can check that there is indeed a satisfying assignment of the eight bits a₀…a₇ (where aᵢ=1 means “vᵢ” chosen, aᵢ=0 means “wᵢ” chosen) with a₄=0 (so w₄ is chosen) that falsifies at least one literal in each bad‐rule body.  Hence there is at least one answer set in which:

  w₄, t₃, t₂, t₁, t₀, wide, q  

are all true, and bad remains false.  

Therefore under STABLE‐MODEL (answer‐set) semantics with CREDULOUS (brave) reasoning, q is true in at least one answer‐set.  

ANSWER: A

First, observe that the only way for q to become true is via the chain

 w4 ⇒ t3 ⇒ t2 ⇒ t1 ⇒ t0 ⇒ q,

together with wide (and s0,s1 which are facts) making wide true, so

 q is true exactly when w4 is true.

All of the other rules governing the v‐ and w‐atoms are in 8 disjoint “default” pairs

 (v0 ∨ w0), (v1 ∨ w1), …, (v7 ∨ w7),

each forced to pick exactly one by the usual even‐cycle default‐negation loops

 (“w_i ← not v_i” and “v_i ← not w_i”).

Hence in principle there are 2^8 = 256 candidate ways to choose which v_i or w_i is true.  Once those are chosen, one checks a large list of “bad‐rules” of the form

 bad ← A, not bad

whose effect under answer‐set (stable‐model) semantics is to forbid any assignment that makes all of the atoms in any single condition A simultaneously true.  If an assignment survives (avoids all those forbidden triples A), it is a stable model.

Because w4 and v4 sit in exactly one such default pair, there are—in any surviving stable model—exactly two possibilities:

  • w4 = true (hence q = true), or  
  • v4 = true (hence w4 = false and q = false),

provided that choice does not trigger any “bad” rule.  One can check (and indeed one finds) that at least one stable model survives with w4 true and at least one survives with w4 false.  Thus q is true in some answer sets and false in others.

1. q is true ⇔ t₀ is true ∧ wide is true.  
2. wide is unconditionally true because s₀ and s₁ are both asserted true.  
3. t₀ is true ⇔ t₁ is true ⇔ t₂ is true ⇔ t₃ is true ⇔ w₄ is true.  
   Hence t₀ ≡ w₄.  

So q ≡ w₄ ∧ true, i.e. q ≡ w₄. We only need the well‐founded truth of w₄.

Let’s simplify systematically.

1.  From  
   “v4 is true if w4 is not true”  and  
   “w4 is true if v4 is not true”  
   we get exactly one of v4,w4 is true and the other false (v4 ↔ ¬w4, w4 ↔ ¬v4).  

2.  Likewise each of the eight pairs  
   (v0,w0), (v1,w1), (v2,w2), (v3,w3), (v5,w5), (v6,w6), (v7,w7), (v4,w4)  
   is linked by the same “each is true iff the other is false.”  So each pair is an independent binary choice.  

3.  The “bad” rules all have the form  
   “bad is true if (a 4‐atom conjunction) and bad is not true,”  
   which logically is equivalent to “bad is true if that conjunction holds.”  No rule for bad feeds back to force any of the xi, wi variables to a unique value; bad is just a derived OR of many possible 4‐tuples.  

4.  The only rule for q is  
   q is true if w4 and wide and etrue.  
   We know etrue is given true, and wide = s0∧s1∧s2 is given true.  So q ⇔ w4.  

5.  But w4 is still free to be either true or false (it merely XOR’s with v4).  Hence q can be either true or false depending on that one independent choice.  

Conclusion: q cannot be definitively assigned.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s restate the critical dependencies for q:

1. q is true if and only if w4 ∧ wide ∧ etrue.  
   – etrue is given true.  
   – wide requires s0, s1, s2, all of which are given true.  
   ⇒ q reduces to checking w4.  

2. w4 has exactly one clause:  
   w4 ← not v4.

3. v4 has exactly one clause:  
   v4 ← not w4.

These two clauses form a direct negation‐loop.  Under Prolog‐style negation‐as‐failure:

– To prove w4, we must show v4 fails.  
– To show v4 fails, we try to prove v4, which in turn requires showing w4 fails.  
– That goes back to proving w4, etc., ad infinitum.

There is no terminating proof of w4, nor a finite failure, so the system flounders.  Hence we cannot determine w4, and thus cannot determine q.

We restate the program more compactly and observe that

– s0,s1,s2 and etrue are unconditional facts, so wide ← s0,s1,s2 makes wide true in every answer set.  
– q ← w4,wide,etrue reduces to q ← w4, so q holds exactly in those answer‐sets that choose w4 rather than v4.  
– For each i=0…7 there is the “toggle” pair

     vi ← not wi.  
     wi ← not vi.

  so each answer set picks exactly one of vi,wi.  
– bad has many rules of the form

     bad ← Body, not bad

  i.e. bad must be true if any one Body‐conjunction is fully satisfied.  But under stable‐model semantics any model that puts bad=true would lose all those rules in its Gelfond–Lifschitz reduct (they all contain “not bad”), so bad could not be derived in the reduct ­– hence no model can contain bad.  Thus every stable model sets bad=false, and it must avoid satisfying *any* of the Bodies in those “bad” rules.

Hence answer‐sets are exactly the 2⁸ assignments to the toggles vi/wi that never make any of the forbidden conjunctions Body entirely true.  In particular we only need to exhibit one satisfying assignment with w4=true (so q=true) that falsifies at least one literal in each bad‐Body.

Here is one such assignment of the toggles (v = true means pick vi, w = true means pick wi):

  v0 = false, w0 = true  
  v1 = false, w1 = true  
  v2 = true,  w2 = false  
  v3 = false, w3 = true  
  v4 = false, w4 = true   ←→  q  
  v5 = true,  w5 = false  
  v6 = false, w6 = true  
  v7 = false, w7 = true  

Together with the facts s0,s1,s2,etrue this assignment falsifies at least one atom in *every* bad‐rule‐body, so none of the “bad” rules fires, giving bad=false consistently.  It also makes w4=true, so wide=true and q=true.  One checks that this set is indeed a stable model of the full program.  Hence q is true in at least one answer set.

Therefore, under credulous (brave) reasoning, q is derivable.

Let us recast the “bad”‐rules as clauses over the eight Boolean choices X₀…X₇, where Xᵢ = true means vᵢ is in the candidate and Xᵢ = false means wᵢ is.  (Since for each i we have “vᵢ ← not wᵢ” and “wᵢ ← not vᵢ,” exactly one of vᵢ,wᵢ must hold in any answer set.)  A “bad” rule of the form

  bad :- A, B, C, not bad.

after checking that bad itself cannot survive in the reduct unless it has a non‐default rule, simply means that if A,B,C all hold then bad would have to be in the model—contradiction—so to have a stable model we must falsify at least one of A,B,C.  Each triple conjoins three of the literals vᵢ or wⱼ, which under X‐notation become either Xᵢ or ¬Xᵢ.  Thus each bad‐rule becomes a 3‐literal “blocking clause” of the form

  ¬(lit₁ ∧ lit₂ ∧ lit₃)
  
↔ (¬lit₁ ∨ ¬lit₂ ∨ ¬lit₃),

and we must satisfy *all* such clauses to avoid forcing bad.  In addition the exclusive laws Xᵢ ∨ ¬Xᵢ must hold, and the facts s₀,s₁,s₂ and etrue make wide true.  Finally

  q :- w₄, wide, etrue

becomes

  q ↔ ¬X₄

since wide and etrue are unconditionally true.  Hence q is in every answer set exactly if in every solution of the 32 blocking‐clauses we have X₄=0.

One can check (and indeed no truth‐assignment to X₀…X₇ can satisfy *all* 32 clauses simultaneously) that the system is *inconsistent*—there is no way to avoid at least one of the “bad” conjunctions.  Consequently *there are no stable models at all*. Let’s focus on q.  We have:

1. s0, s1, s2, etrue are all unconditionally true.  
2. wide ← s0 ∧ s1 ∧ s2  ⇒ wide = true.  
3. q ← w4 ∧ wide ∧ etrue ⇒ q has exactly the same well-founded value as w4.
